essays.stem: A Jamaican company that makes hot pepper sauces wants to grow sales in local supermarkets and among tourists over the next six months, with J$1,500,000 to spend. Prepare an outline promotion plan.
essays.modelAnswer: The aims would be to raise supermarket sales by 15% and to get the sauces into ten hotel and airport gift shops within six months. There are two audiences: Jamaican household shoppers and visitors looking for local gifts. The key message for locals is real Jamaican flavour made with Scotch bonnet peppers; for visitors it is 'take a taste of Jamaica home'. Activities would include in-store tastings and point-of-sale displays in the main supermarket chains (J$450,000), social media adverts and recipe videos with a local cook (J$400,000), gift packs and display stands for hotel and airport shops (J$350,000), and a stand at a food and tourism trade fair (J$200,000), with J$100,000 held as contingency. The timing would build towards the Christmas season and the winter tourist season. Results would be measured monthly by sales by outlet, the number of new outlets, the cost per new outlet, engagement on social media and coupon use at tastings. The plan would be reviewed after three months and money moved to what works best.
markingPoints: Sets measurable aims and identifies the target audiences
Gives clear key messages suited to each audience
Chooses suitable activities and shows a budget that adds up to J$1,500,000
Plans the timing around key seasons
Sets measures and a review point to adjust the plan

essays.stem: Compare traditional media (radio, newspapers and billboards) with digital media for promoting a small business in rural Jamaica, and recommend a mix.
essays.modelAnswer: Radio is still widely heard in rural Jamaica, especially on local and talk stations, so it reaches many people at once and builds trust. However, radio time can be costly, it is hard to target, and results are hard to track. Newspapers reach older readers and suit detailed offers, but readership is falling. Billboards on main roads give steady awareness but carry little information and cost a great deal. Digital media, such as social media, messaging apps and search listings, cost less, can be aimed at people by area, age and interest, and give clear figures such as reach, clicks and enquiries. Their weaknesses are that some older customers use them less, the content needs regular work, and posts can be lost among many others. For a small rural business with a limited budget, I would recommend mainly digital promotion, including an accurate map listing and a WhatsApp business number, supported by a few short spots on a local radio station and simple signs at the business. I would track enquiries from each channel and adjust the mix.
markingPoints: Explains the strengths and limits of radio, newspapers and billboards
Explains the strengths and limits of digital media
Considers the rural audience, the budget and the ability to measure results
Makes a clear recommendation for a mix of media
Says how the mix would be monitored and adjusted

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can judge whether a promotional campaign was worth its cost.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the manager must have set measurable aims before the campaign started, such as 200 new enquiries or a 10% rise in sales, and taken a baseline of results before it began. During the campaign, each channel should be tracked with its own code, link or phone number, so results can be linked to the activity that caused them. The manager would then measure outputs, such as reach, engagement and coupon redemption, and, more importantly, outcomes, such as enquiries, conversion rate, sales and new customers. The key test is financial: the extra gross profit earned compared with the full cost of the campaign, including staff time and discounts given. For example, if a campaign cost J$200,000 and brought in J$300,000 of extra gross profit, the return is 50%. The manager should also allow for other causes, such as the season or a competitor closing, and for longer-term effects, such as brand awareness, which could be measured by a survey. The findings would be written up with lessons for the next campaign.
markingPoints: Sets measurable aims and a baseline before the campaign
Tracks each channel so results can be traced
Measures outcomes such as enquiries, conversion and sales, not just reach
Compares extra profit with the full cost to find the return
Allows for other causes and longer-term effects and records the lessons

essays.stem: Explain the main legal and ethical points a manager must consider when promoting a business in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: Promotion must be honest. Consumer protection law, in general terms, does not allow claims that mislead customers about price, quality or what a product does, so every claim should be one the business can prove. Prices in adverts should be clear, with GCT shown at the current rate where it applies, and offer conditions, such as end dates and limits, stated plainly. Intellectual property law means the business must not use other people's music, photos, logos or written work without permission, and must not copy a rival's brand. The data protection law means personal data, such as phone numbers and e-mail addresses, should be collected for a clear purpose, kept secure and used for marketing only where customers have agreed, with an easy way to opt out. Paid endorsements by influencers should be shown as paid. On ethics, promotions aimed at children, or for alcohol, gambling or unhealthy products, need special care and any industry rules must be followed. Comparisons with competitors must be fair and true. A manager should check promotions against company policy before they run.
markingPoints: Claims must be true and not misleading, in line with consumer protection law
Prices, GCT and offer conditions must be clear
Respects intellectual property: permission for music, images and brands
Follows data protection aims: consent, purpose, security and opt-out
Considers ethics such as targeting children, paid endorsements and fair comparisons

essays.stem: Compare three methods of setting a promotion budget and recommend one for a growing business.
essays.modelAnswer: The percentage-of-sales method sets the budget as a share of past or expected sales, such as 3%. It is simple and easy to afford, but it is backwards, because sales are a result of promotion, and it cuts spending just when sales are falling and more promotion may be needed. The competitive parity method matches what competitors spend. It helps a business keep up its share of attention, but competitors' figures are hard to know, and their aims and position may be quite different. The objective-and-task method starts from the promotion aims, lists the activities needed to reach them and adds up their costs. It links spending directly to results and makes the manager justify each activity. Its weakness is that it takes more work and can produce a total the business cannot afford. For a growing business, I would recommend the objective-and-task method, because it ties spending to growth targets, checked against what the business can afford and adjusted as results come in.
markingPoints: Explains the percentage-of-sales method with a strength and a weakness
Explains the competitive parity method with a strength and a weakness
Explains the objective-and-task method with a strength and a weakness
Makes a clear recommendation for a growing business
Justifies the recommendation, including a check on affordability

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up and manage social media to promote a guest house in Treasure Beach.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first set aims, such as 30 direct bookings a month from social media, and decide on the audiences: local weekend visitors and overseas travellers. I would choose two or three platforms where those audiences spend time, rather than trying to be on all of them. Each profile would have the same name, logo, contact details, booking link and a short description of what makes the guest house special. I would plan a content calendar with a mix of posts: photos and short videos of rooms, the beach and local food, guest stories shared with their permission, special offers and local events. Posts would go out on a regular schedule and replies to messages and comments would be given within a few hours. I would deal with complaints politely and move them to private messages. A named staff member would manage the accounts, following a short social media policy. Each month I would check reach, engagement, enquiries and bookings from social media, and change the content that is not working.
markingPoints: Sets aims and identifies the target audiences
Chooses a small number of suitable platforms with consistent branding
Plans varied content with a content calendar
Responds quickly and handles complaints well, under a clear policy
Measures results such as enquiries and bookings and adjusts the plan

essays.stem: Explain how public relations and community involvement can promote a business, with examples, and describe the risks to manage.
essays.modelAnswer: Public relations builds the business's reputation and goodwill rather than selling a product directly. Because news stories and community activity are not seen as paid adverts, people often trust them more. Examples include a press release about a new branch opening that creates local jobs, an interview on a parish radio station, sponsoring a school's prize-giving, staff volunteering in a beach clean-up, or a hardware store running free home-repair workshops. These raise awareness, show the business's values and can lead to word-of-mouth recommendations. There are risks. The business cannot control how the media reports a story. A sponsored event that goes badly, or a partner with a poor reputation, can harm the brand. Community work that looks like a publicity stunt can bring criticism. To manage these risks, the manager should choose causes that fit the business and its customers, check partners carefully, agree terms in writing, prepare key messages and one trained spokesperson, and keep commitments over time rather than once only.
markingPoints: Explains what public relations is and why it can be trusted more than advertising
Gives suitable examples of PR and community activity
Explains the benefits, such as awareness, goodwill and word of mouth
Identifies the risks, such as loss of control, poor partners or seeming insincere
Suggests ways to manage the risks

essays.stem: Compare how you would promote a business that sells to other businesses with one that sells to the public, using examples from Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: A business that sells to other businesses, such as an office supplies firm in Kingston selling to schools and offices, has fewer customers, larger orders and buying decisions made by several people, often against a budget or a tender. Its promotion would rely on personal selling, networking at business groups, trade shows, case studies, direct e-mail to named contacts who have agreed to receive it, and a professional website and business networking profile. The message would stress reliability, cost savings and service. A business that sells to the public, such as a patty shop in Spanish Town, has many customers making quick, small, often emotional decisions. Its promotion would use social media, radio, signs, point-of-sale displays, sales promotions and loyalty rewards, with a short, catchy message about taste, price and convenience. Both need a clear brand and must measure results, but the business seller measures leads and contracts won, while the consumer seller measures footfall, sales and redemption. Budgets also differ: business sellers spend more per customer.
markingPoints: Describes the features of business buyers: few, large, several decision-makers
Gives suitable promotion methods and messages for business buyers
Describes the features of the public as buyers: many, small, quick decisions
Gives suitable promotion methods and messages for the public
Compares how results and budgets differ

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can involve staff in promoting the business, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff are often the face of the business, so what they say and do can promote it or harm it more than any advert. A manager can involve them first by sharing the promotion plan and its aims, so everyone knows what is being promoted and why. Before each campaign, staff should be briefed on the offer, its terms and how to answer questions, and given simple product training. They can be asked for ideas, because front-line staff hear what customers want. Staff can take part in community events, trade shows and social media content, with their agreement and within a clear social media policy. A small reward for referrals or for the best customer feedback can keep interest up. The manager must also make sure staff deliver what the promotion promises, because an advert that brings customers in to poor service wastes the money spent. Involving staff matters because it builds commitment, makes the message consistent, brings in useful ideas and turns good service into word-of-mouth promotion.
markingPoints: Explains that staff are the face of the business and affect its image
Shares the plan and briefs staff before campaigns
Seeks staff ideas and involves them in events and content, under a policy
Links promotion to service delivery so promises are kept
Explains the benefits: commitment, consistency, ideas and word of mouth

essays.stem: Plan how a business would use a trade show to promote itself, from preparation to follow-up.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would decide whether the show is worth it, by checking who attends, the cost of the stand and travel, and whether the visitors are our target customers. If so, I would set aims, such as 80 qualified leads and 10 sales meetings booked. I would design a stand that shows the brand clearly, with a simple display, a screen or samples, and a way to capture visitor details lawfully, such as a sign-up form that asks for consent. I would promote our presence beforehand by inviting existing and target customers. I would choose and brief staff on the aims, the key messages, how to approach visitors and how to record leads, and plan a rota so the stand is always staffed. At the show, staff would engage visitors, qualify leads and note what each wants. Within a week after the show, every lead would be followed up with a personal message, and meetings booked. Finally, I would compare the leads, sales and costs with the aims to decide whether to attend again.
markingPoints: Decides whether the show suits the target customers and budget
Sets measurable aims for the show
Prepares the stand, invitations and lawful lead capture
Briefs and rosters staff and manages the stand well on the day
Follows up leads quickly and evaluates results against cost

practical1.title: Prepare a promotion plan and sample campaign materials for a local business
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case about a made-up Jamaican business (for example a juice bar in Ocho Rios, a hardware store in May Pen or a tour company in Port Antonio), with its customers, competitors and a promotion budget in J$. As a group, prepare a three-month promotion plan and sample materials. Give each member a named role: plan lead (writes the aims, target audience and key message), media planner (chooses the activities and channels and gives reasons), budget officer (builds the budget in a spreadsheet so that it adds up to the amount given, with a contingency, checking every figure twice), designer (produces a poster or flyer and two sample social media posts, using only the group's own words and images or free-to-use material), and measures officer (sets how each activity will be measured, with targets). In a group of four, the plan lead also sets the measures. Finish by presenting the plan to the assessor in 10 minutes as if to the business owner.
materials: Computers with word processor, spreadsheet and simple design software
Flipchart paper, markers and coloured paper
photos: The written aims, target audience and key message
The table of chosen activities and channels with reasons
The budget spreadsheet on screen with the total matching the amount given
The finished poster or flyer and the sample social media posts
The table of measures and targets
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Aims are measurable and the audience and message fit the business
Activities and channels suit the audience and the budget, with reasons
Budget adds up correctly to the amount given and includes a contingency
Materials are clear, honest and use only material the group may use
Measures and targets are set for each activity
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use made-up names; do not copy real brands, logos or other people's images
Treat the case data as confidential and return printouts to the assessor
Respect each other's ideas and share the workload fairly
Take a short break away from the screen during the task

practical2.title: Evaluate a campaign's results and pitch a better plan for next quarter
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a spreadsheet of results from a made-up business's last promotional campaign: for each channel (for example radio, flyers, social media adverts, a trade fair and a referral offer), the cost, reach, enquiries, sales and gross profit. As a group, work out how well each channel did and pitch a better plan for next quarter. Give each member a named role: data analyst (works out cost per enquiry, conversion rate and return for each channel in the spreadsheet, checking every figure twice), chart maker (makes a clear chart comparing the channels), evaluator (writes what the figures show and what they do not, such as effects on brand awareness or the season), planner (proposes how to move the budget between channels next quarter, with targets), and presenter (leads a 10-minute pitch to the assessor, playing the business owner, with help from the others). In a group of four, the evaluator also presents.
materials: Campaign results spreadsheet from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and presentation software
photos: The spreadsheet on screen with cost per enquiry, conversion and return for each channel
The evaluator's notes on what the figures do and do not show
The new budget split with targets for next quarter
The pitch slides or flipchart and the group presenting
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the work
Cost per enquiry, conversion rate and return are correct for each channel
Chart is clear, labelled and fair
Evaluation notes the limits of the data, not just the figures
New plan moves money for clear reasons and sets targets
Answered the owner's questions politely and with evidence
safety: Treat the campaign data as confidential business information
Keep comments about the made-up business's staff respectful and factual
Share the workload fairly and support members who are less confident with spreadsheets
Take a short break away from the screen during the task
